title: CEO Interview with Chuck McClish of of Lattrex Inc. - Semiwiki
gist: Lattrex, a one-man fabless startup founded by 15-year Microchip veteran Chuck McClish, is betting that an asynchronous, clockless, homogeneous coarse-grained reconfigurable array (Kyttar) beats DSPs and FPGAs for many-channel, low-power real-time signal processing. A 120-cell prototype taped out solo in three months returns from the fab in fall 2026, with software-defined radio and defense/electronic-warfare as the beachhead and the placeKYT toolchain — not the silicon — treated as the real bottleneck.

insights.claim: Lattrex's entire thesis is that the semiconductor industry took an unnecessarily complicated path by optimizing around the clock for decades, and that asynchronous self-timed design was skipped for reasons of tooling, talent and momentum rather than because it failed technically.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A credible-founder revival of clockless logic is a low-probability/high-payoff option on a design paradigm the incumbent EDA and FPGA stack cannot easily copy; watch whether any tooling ecosystem forms around it.
insights.quote: Lattrex is built on a bet, and the bet is that the industry took the more complicated road when a simpler one was right there.

insights.claim: The Kyttar architecture was derived from a biology analogy: fine-grained parallelism with local communication and no centralized control, the mechanism nature uses to scale organisms from amoeba to blue whale, transplanted into a silicon compute substrate where programs 'grow' like mycelium.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating scaling claims in novel compute: ask whether control is centralized, because centralized control is what caps graceful scaling.
insights.quote: a compute substrate where programs grow, not unlike fungal mycelium spreading across a petri dish
insights.locator: So I ran a thought experiment

insights.claim: Contemporary chip design is framed as fundamentally unscalable because every chip is a bespoke artifact — 'a custom work of art' that is complex, fragile and does not scale gracefully — a diagnosis that motivates homogeneity as the fix.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Frames rising design cost/NRE as a structural problem, supporting the broader investment case for tiled, replicated architectures over monolithic custom SoCs.
insights.quote: Every chip is essentially a custom work of art. Each one is enormously complex, fragile, and typically doesn’t scale gracefully.
insights.locator: While working on various unrelated projects

themes.theme: The DSP/FPGA gap in edge signal processing

insights.claim: The addressable gap is that neither of the two default tools for edge real-time signal processing fits many-channel low-power workloads: a DSP is approachable but serial and hits a throughput wall, while an FPGA is parallel but costs clock-tree power, HDL and timing-closure effort, and long design cycles.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defines the exact wedge a new architecture must attack — and by extension the FPGA/DSP revenue pools (AMD/Xilinx, Lattice, Microchip, TI-class parts) most exposed if a third path works.
insights.quote: A DSP is approachable but fundamentally serial, so you hit a throughput wall. An FPGA is parallel and powerful but you pay for it in clock-tree power, in HDL and timing closure, and in long design cycles.

insights.claim: The stated demand driver is that through the 2030s an increasing share of real-time signal processing is being pushed to locations with almost no power or space budget, expanding the class of workloads that clocked monolithic parts serve badly.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A secular SWaP-constrained edge trend is the tailwind the whole thesis rides on; if it holds, low-idle-power parallel silicon is a growing category regardless of who wins it.
insights.quote: As we move toward the 2030s, more and more real-time signal processing is being pushed out to places with almost no power or space to spare.

insights.claim: Lattrex concedes it loses on single-channel peak performance — a DSP or FPGA beats its architecture today if the task is pushing one channel as fast as possible — and competes only on many parallel, mostly-idle channels where idle power dominates.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: An unusually candid boundary condition: the metric to benchmark against incumbents is idle/aggregate channel power, not throughput per channel.
insights.quote: If you need to push one channel as fast as possible, a DSP or an FPGA will win vs our architecture today. We’re playing a different game.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: The architecture is positioned as a coarse-grained reconfigurable array sitting between a DSP's flexibility and an FPGA's parallelism, differentiated by being self-timed and homogeneous — properties claimed to compound rather than trade off against each other.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Places Lattrex in the CGRA category, a long-attempted middle ground; the compounding-not-trading claim is the falsifiable part to test against first silicon data.
insights.quote: for many parallel, mostly-idle channels in a constrained power and size budget, the idle power is the story
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

themes.theme: Homogeneity as a manufacturing and verification lever

insights.claim: The deepest claimed differentiation is not the circuit but the manufacturing and verification model: one simple cell verified once and tiled endlessly, versus an industry path of ever-increasing per-chip complexity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: If verification cost collapses to one cell, NRE and time-to-tapeout — the dominant costs in advanced-node design — become the real competitive moat, not PPA.
insights.quote: one simple cell, verified once, tiled endlessly, which is a fundamentally different bet than the ever-more-complex path the rest of the industry is on
insights.locator: The deeper differentiation is the manufacturing

insights.claim: Because the array is a sea of identical cells, manufacturing defects can be routed around at programming time rather than mitigated with dedicated redundancy hardware, which is pitched as a yield and radiation-tolerance advantage for harsh-environment and space applications.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defect-tolerance-by-software is a genuine cost lever at advanced nodes and a credible entry point into rad-hard/space markets where incumbents charge large premiums.
insights.quote: a defective one can be routed around at programming time instead of designed around with redundancy hardware

insights.claim: Software-defined radio is the declared beachhead market, with spectrum monitoring, multi-channel phased-array receivers and electronic-warfare defense applications as the named adjacencies.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals that the first revenue, if any, comes from defense electronics budgets rather than commercial edge AI — a different funding and timeline profile.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: The buyer pain in SDR and defense is described as simultaneous SWaP-budget pressure and long toolchain cycles, with the specific desired outcomes being changing a waveform without rebuilding a bitstream, adding channels without growing the power envelope, and going from idea to working hardware in under a quarter.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: These three requirements are the concrete acceptance criteria to judge Lattrex or any competing CGRA against — especially the sub-quarter idea-to-hardware bar.
insights.quote: They want to change a waveform without rebuilding a bitstream, add channels without growing the power envelope, and get from idea to working hardware in less than a quarter.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: Lattrex is funding and validating the defense path through an SBIR/STTR track alongside open, self-serve engagement via publicly downloadable tooling, rather than through a traditional enterprise sales motion.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Non-dilutive government funding plus developer-led adoption is the standard survival path for deep-tech silicon startups; SBIR award news would be the first external validation signal.

insights.claim: Lattrex explicitly states the most important thing it is building is not the next chip but the usability of the architecture, on the reasoning that an asynchronous reconfigurable array is worthless if nobody can program it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Confirms the recurring lesson from novel-silicon failures: software adoption, not tapeout, is the gating milestone to track.
insights.quote: An async reconfigurable array is worthless if nobody can program it, so tackling programmability is the first thing I’m doing.

insights.claim: The placeKYT development environment piggybacks on GNU Radio Companion as the design entry point, then places, routes and simulates against a cycle-accurate model with instruction-level debug and speed/power estimates, and the same flow is intended to drive real silicon when first parts return.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Adopting an existing open SDR front-end instead of a proprietary HDL lowers the switching cost for the exact engineers in the target market — the cheapest possible distribution strategy.

insights.claim: The publicly available placeKYT examples already demonstrate end-to-end placed, routed and simulated designs including a gain block, single-sideband, AM and FM transceivers, and a BPSK modem — concrete evidence the toolchain handles complete signal chains pre-silicon.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A verifiable, downloadable artifact — the cheapest independent due-diligence check available on this company's claims today.

themes.theme: Company stage, silicon timeline and roadmap

insights.claim: Lattrex is effectively a solo operation — a fabless startup that is 'mostly me and a lot of tooling' — whose founder Chuck McClish, a 15-year Microchip Technology veteran who worked nearly every seat of the design flow from RTL and UVM verification through place-and-route and STA, designed and taped out the first Kyttar prototype alone in three months.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Single-founder tapeout capability lowers the capital floor for novel-architecture silicon, expanding the universe of credible seed-stage semiconductor bets — while concentrating all key-man risk in one person.
insights.quote: Right now Lattrex is a fabless startup that’s mostly me and a lot of tooling, with a 120-cell prototype chip coming back from the fab this fall.
insights.locator: Right now Lattrex is a fabless startup

insights.claim: The first Kyttar silicon is a 120-cell prototype with first parts returning at the end of November 2026, making that tapeout return the binary near-term proof point for the whole asynchronous-array thesis.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable milestone: measured idle power and cell yield on the 120-cell part in late 2026 either validates or kills the differentiation claims.

insights.claim: The stated roadmap past first silicon is a performance-optimized cell on a modern FinFET node with far more cells per die, then pairing the array with an analog front-end die so the full antenna-to-bits signal chain lives in one package.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The endgame is a single-package RF-to-digital receiver, which would put Lattrex in direct competition with integrated RF SoC vendors rather than just FPGA/DSP suppliers.
insights.quote: eventually pairing the array with an analog front-end die so the whole signal chain, antenna to bits, lives in one package
insights.locator: Past that, the roadmap is to develop
